# Results — Study 49 (Black-Gold): does oil predict the stock market? 2000–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly returns of **WTI crude (CL=F)** and
the **S&P 500 (^GSPC)**, 2000-09 → 2026-06 (220 months). Driesprong et al. (2008): last month's oil
return forecasts this month's equity return, negatively. As-of 2026-06; inputs fingerprint `d0da64757640`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `NONE` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Replicates out of sample"? `BUSTED`

The famous oil-predicts-stocks result **does not survive into the era you'd trade it**. Regressing this
month's equity return on last month's oil return gives a slope of **+0.017 (t = +0.6)** — *insignificant
and the wrong sign* (Driesprong's effect is **negative**). A timing rule that holds equities after oil
falls earns **Sharpe 0.26** against buy-and-hold's **0.42** — it badly underperforms by sitting in cash
half the time for no edge. And it was never there in the modern data: the slope is insignificant in both
the 2000–2008 and 2009-on subsamples, positive throughout. `BUSTED`.

## Data stamp

- **Pair**: WTI (CL=F) + S&P 500 (^GSPC) monthly, 2000-09 → 2026-06, 220 months, fingerprint `d0da64757640`

## No predictive relationship — and the sign is wrong

| regress equity_t on oil_(t−1) | value |
|---|---|
| slope | **+0.017** (Driesprong: negative) |
| correlation | +0.043 |
| t-stat | **+0.6** |

A t of 0.6 is indistinguishable from zero, and the *sign* is the opposite of the claim. Whatever
Driesprong found in 1973–2003, the relationship is absent in every month of tradable oil-futures data.

## …and the timing rule trails buy-and-hold

| | CAGR | Sharpe | max-DD | time in market |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| oil timing (long after oil falls) | +2.2% | **0.26** | −38% | 46% |
| buy & hold S&P | +5.1% | **0.42** | −41% | 100% |

Conditioning equity exposure on last month's oil halves your return and lowers your Sharpe — you sit in
cash 54% of the time to dodge a danger that isn't there.

## It was never significant in the modern sample

| | slope | t |
|---|---|---|
| 2000–2008 | +0.017 | +0.3 |
| 2009–on | +0.005 | +0.2 |

No sub-period shows the negative, significant relationship the strategy needs. The cross-asset signal —
if it ever existed — did not carry into the 21st century.

## The honest takeaway

"Oil predicts the stock market" is a `MIRAGE` on every month of tradable data: the predictive slope is
insignificant and the wrong sign, and the timing rule underperforms buy-and-hold while holding cash half
the time. The original 1973–2003 result doesn't replicate out of sample — a textbook reminder that a
documented predictability is a hypothesis about the *future*, and this one failed it. `NONE`, `MIRAGE`,
`BUSTED`.
